title: Governing for Student Success
author: Kunjan Narechania
summary: Published on Election Day as a guest piece for Aneesh Sohoni's Leadership Launchpad, Kunjan Narechania, CEO of Watershed Advisors and former leader of New Orleans' Recovery School District, advises newly elected governors to make education a signature issue. She points to Massachusetts in the 1990s and Tennessee since 2009 as states where sustained gubernatorial leadership across administrations lifted student achievement. Her advice has three parts: set a clear vision tied to the voters' priorities such as affordability, workforce, AI readiness, youth mental health, and teacher shortages; spend money, time, and the bully pulpit on that vision; and build infrastructure now even if results arrive after the term ends. She stresses that a governor need not design every policy but must make priorities clear, meet regularly with the education chief, and coordinate across agencies. The piece frames legacy as whether students are better off, not how many initiatives were launched.
points: Education is presented as a means to a governor's other goals, from affordability to workforce to AI readiness, which makes it a signature issue and not a side portfolio.
Massachusetts and Tennessee show that progress came from sustained leadership across governors, not from one term.
Prioritization means aligning the budget, the calendar, and the bully pulpit, including regular check-ins with the education chief.
Many education solutions need coordination across education, workforce, and economic development agencies that only a governor can convene.
Building durable systems and accountability matters more than immediate wins, because the next governor can carry them forward.
quotes: Few things you do as governor will have a bigger impact on the long-term future of your state than improving its schools. And we’ve seen the difference governors can make when they treat education as a priority.
What made the difference was sustained leadership: governors who made education a priority, built on the work of their predecessors, and stayed the course.
As governor, the name of the game is prioritization. Once you’ve decided what you want to accomplish, your time, money, and political capital need to follow.
Make education a regular part of your schedule, not something you only check in on when there’s a crisis.

You don’t need to personally design every education policy. But you do need to make your priorities clear, put the resources of your office behind them, and keep everyone moving in the same direction.
Especially when changes are difficult or unpopular, governors have an important role to play in explaining why they matter and building public support.

The governors who leave the biggest mark on education aren’t necessarily the ones who can point to immediate wins. They’re the ones willing to build something that the next governor can pick up and carry forward.
